modalities.name: Today's Faces Round
modalities.tagline: Evening goodwill for the people you actually met today.
modalities.whatItIs: Today's Faces Round offers goodwill only to the people you crossed paths with today, from the bus driver to a colleague, in a short self-led evening sit. Where Ideal Parent Figure work uses a therapist and imagined ideal figures to revisit childhood, this stays with real people and with today. It is a proposed practice that needs no teacher, script or recording.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill can grow from real, recent encounters rather than from imagined figures or the distant past, so the practice stays in today and in your own hands.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before bed, sit for 10 to 15 minutes and replay your day in order, pausing on each person you met, however briefly, and silently wishing them well with a phrase such as 'may your evening be easy'. People you only glimpsed count too, and if a face stirs strong irritation you note that and move on to the next one. You end by including yourself as the last face of the day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find classic loving-kindness too abstract or sentimental, and anyone who wants a simple, self-led way to end the day feeling more connected to the people around them.
modalities.cautions: Wishing people well can stir up irritation, grief or a sense of not deserving kindness, so keep sessions short and skip any face that brings strong distress. It is an untested idea; if old hurts keep surfacing, talk with a therapist rather than pushing on alone.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Today's Faces Round. Before bed, replay your day and silently wish each person you met well: the barista, the bus driver, a coworker, then yourself. Self-led, 10 minutes, no teacher needed. For anyone who finds loving-kindness too abstract.

modalities.name: Hundred-Count Wish
modalities.tagline: One kind phrase, counted a hundred times, and nothing else.
modalities.whatItIs: Hundred-Count Wish builds a whole practice out of a single goodwill phrase, repeated exactly one hundred times and counted on beads, fingers or a hand clicker. Internal Family Systems turns toward many inner voices with curiosity; this proposed practice keeps to one steady voice, one phrase and no inner conversation at all. It is self-led, calm and takes about 15 minutes.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that simplicity steadies attention: when the whole practice is one phrase and one count, there is nothing to negotiate, and the phrase can settle in through repetition.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose one phrase, such as 'may I be at ease', and sit comfortably with a string of beads or a hand counter. Repeat the phrase silently and slowly, moving one bead for each repetition, until you reach one hundred. When a doubting or critical thought appears, you neither argue with it nor explore it; you simply say the next phrase and move the next bead.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel swamped by open-ended meditation or by long lists of instructions, and those who like a practice with a clear finish line.
modalities.cautions: Repetition can feel mechanical, and kind words aimed at yourself sometimes bring up their opposite, such as a sense of unworthiness, so switch to a phrase for someone easy to love if that happens. If a critical inner voice keeps returning strongly, a therapist can help you understand it rather than talk over it; this is an untested idea, not a replacement for care.
modalities.tweet: An idea for busy minds: Hundred-Count Wish. One kind phrase, like 'may I be at ease', repeated 100 times on beads or a clicker. No inner debate, no steps to remember, just the count. About 15 minutes, done alone.

modalities.name: Wordless Warmth
modalities.tagline: Goodwill felt as warmth in the body, with no phrases at all.
modalities.whatItIs: Wordless Warmth is an untested version of loving-kindness that drops the phrases and the reasoning and lets goodwill become a plain bodily feeling. Compared with the talking, analyzing and worksheets of cognitive behavioral therapy, it is looser, calmer and felt rather than thought. There is no set sequence to follow.
modalities.coreIdea: Kindness can be felt before it is put into words, so the practice rests in a warm feeling instead of reasoning or repeating sentences.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down or sit comfortably, bring to mind someone easy to love for a moment, and notice any warmth or softening in the chest, face or hands. Let the image fade and stay with that warmth for 10 to 20 minutes, letting it spread or ebb as it likes. When thoughts start to argue or explain, you do not dispute them; you return to the feeling.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find repeated phrases stiff or who already spend a lot of time analyzing their thoughts, and anyone who wants a softer, wordless way into goodwill.
modalities.cautions: Some people feel little or nothing at first, which is normal, while others find that warmth brings tears or grief, so keep sessions short and stop if it becomes overwhelming. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for therapy for depression or anxiety.
modalities.tweet: What if kindness didn't need words? Wordless Warmth is a new idea: picture someone easy to love, then let the image go and rest in the warmth it leaves in your chest. No phrases, no analysis, 10 to 20 minutes lying down.

modalities.name: Joy Staircase
modalities.tagline: Climb, step by step, from a small pleasant feeling to deep calm.
modalities.whatItIs: Joy Staircase turns the traditional path into meditative absorption into a short, structured ladder: a small pleasant feeling, then gladness, then contentment, then still calm. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy asks you to make room for whatever you feel and to act on your values, while this proposed practice deliberately builds one chosen inner state for its own sake. It is done alone, sitting, with a fixed sequence of steps.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that pleasant, settled states can be trained like a skill, one stable step at a time, rather than simply waited for.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 to 30 minutes and first steady your attention on the breath for about five minutes. Then recall something that reliably makes you smile, find the pleasant feeling it creates in the body and let it grow into gladness; once that holds steady, let it soften into contentment, and then into calm. You move up a step only when the current one feels stable, and you stop wherever you are when the time is up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already meditate a little and want a clear map toward deep calm and enjoyment, and those curious about absorption states but put off by long retreats.
modalities.cautions: Pushing for pleasant states can turn into striving and frustration, and deep concentration sometimes brings strong energy, unusual body sensations or altered states, so stay gentle and learn the deeper stages from an experienced teacher. People with a history of psychosis, mania or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Joy Staircase. A 20-minute sit that climbs on purpose from a small pleasant feeling to gladness, contentment and calm, moving up only when each step feels steady. For meditators who want deep calm without a long retreat. #meditation

modalities.name: Lights-Out Goodwill
modalities.tagline: A slow, soothing wish for everyone under your roof at bedtime.
modalities.whatItIs: Lights-Out Goodwill is a bedtime idea that uses loving-kindness purely to settle down, with no digging into why you feel the way you do. It is the mirror image of Coherence Therapy, which deliberately uncovers the emotional truth behind a problem with a therapist: here everything stays in the present, calm and self-led. It takes 5 to 15 minutes in bed.
modalities.coreIdea: At the end of the day, steady kindness can be used to wind down rather than to work anything out.
modalities.whatYouDo: With the lights out, breathe slowly and on each out-breath silently offer one soft wish, starting with yourself and then each person or pet sleeping under your roof, such as 'may you rest well'. Let the phrases slow and grow quieter until there are long pauses between them and you simply rest. If a worry or a question about the day comes up, you leave it for tomorrow and return to the next wish.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds start reviewing and analyzing as soon as their head hits the pillow, and anyone who wants a gentle, self-led bedtime ritual.
modalities.cautions: If sleep problems or night-time worry last more than a few weeks, talk to a doctor, since this is an untested idea and not a sleep treatment. If strong feelings come up instead of calm, sit up, turn on a light and stop for the night.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea for restless nights: Lights-Out Goodwill. In bed, one slow wish per out-breath for you and everyone under your roof, getting quieter until you just rest. No analyzing the day, no app, 5 to 15 minutes. 🌙

modalities.name: Imagined Gift Giving
modalities.tagline: In your mind's eye, give each person exactly what they need.
modalities.whatItIs: In Imagined Gift Giving, goodwill is expressed entirely through imagination: you picture choosing a fitting gift for each person in turn and handing it over. Tension and trauma releasing exercises let the body lead and shake on its own; this concept leaves the body out completely and works only with mind and imagery. It is done sitting, alone, for about 20 minutes.
modalities.coreIdea: Imagining a concrete act of generosity can make goodwill specific and warm, and it engages the imagination instead of the body.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit with eyes closed, bring to mind one person at a time, starting with someone easy to love, and ask what they most need right now: rest, a warm coat, a good laugh, more time. Picture choosing that gift, handing it over and seeing them receive it, then move on to the next person, widening to neutral people, someone difficult and finally everyone. End by imagining someone handing a fitting gift to you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a vivid imagination who find plain phrases flat, and anyone who wants goodwill to feel more concrete and practical.
modalities.cautions: Picturing what others lack can tip into worry or guilt about what you cannot really give, so keep the gifts light and come back to the feeling of giving. This untested idea is not a way to make peace with someone who harmed you, so leave such people out unless you choose otherwise with a therapist's support.
modalities.tweet: A proposal: Imagined Gift Giving. Eyes closed, picture each person in turn and hand them exactly what they need right now: rest, a warm coat, a good laugh. Then imagine someone handing one to you. Goodwill made concrete, all in the mind's eye.

modalities.name: Crafted Wish Cards
modalities.tagline: Write your own goodwill phrases, word by carefully chosen word.
modalities.whatItIs: Crafted Wish Cards is a proposed practice of composing your own goodwill phrases on purpose, writing them on cards and reciting them in short daily sits. Focusing waits patiently for the right word to arise from a vague bodily sense; here you choose the words deliberately and use them to build a feeling. It is structured and mostly mental, learned from a short guide or teacher and then practiced alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Words you have chosen yourself can carry more meaning than borrowed ones, and writing them down makes the intention deliberate and repeatable.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week, pick one person and spend 10 minutes writing a short wish that fits their life exactly, revising it until every word feels right, for example 'may your new job feel lighter by spring'. Each day, sit for 10 minutes, read the card once, then repeat the wish silently while picturing the person. Keep the cards, and after a few weeks you have a small deck of wishes for the people in your life.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like writing, find stock phrases generic, or want their goodwill to feel personal and specific.
modalities.cautions: Writing a wish for someone you are in conflict with can stir anger or hurt, so start with easy people and leave out anyone who has harmed you unless you choose otherwise with support. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for therapy.
modalities.tweet: New practice idea: Crafted Wish Cards. Once a week, write one short wish for someone and revise it until every word fits their life. Then repeat it in a 10-minute daily sit. Goodwill in your own words, not borrowed ones.

modalities.name: Eight-Week Warmth Ladder
modalities.tagline: A self-run plan that trains goodwill from easy people to hard ones.
modalities.whatItIs: Eight-Week Warmth Ladder is a self-run training plan for goodwill that moves one rung harder each week and tracks how warm each sit felt. Unlike Aletheia Coaching, which lets experience unfold openly with a coach and aims at unfoldment rather than self-improvement, it uses a fixed written plan, measurable targets and no coach at all. Sessions last 15 minutes, done alone on most days of the week.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that goodwill can be built the way fitness is, through a written progression from easy to hard with honest tracking along the way.
modalities.whatYouDo: The rungs run from yourself, a good friend and a neutral acquaintance to someone mildly difficult, a whole group such as your street, and finally everyone, one rung per week plus two review weeks. Before and after each 15-minute sit you rate the warmth you feel from 0 to 10 in a notebook. You move up only when the after-sit ratings have held steady for most of the week, and otherwise you repeat the rung.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like plans, numbers and visible progress, and those who drop meditation because they never know whether they are getting anywhere.
modalities.cautions: Ratings will stall or dip at times, which is information rather than failure, and moving too fast to a hard person can backfire, so never put someone who seriously harmed you on the ladder without support. If self-criticism or low mood grows, slow down and talk to a professional; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Speculative practice: an Eight-Week Warmth Ladder. Train goodwill like fitness, one rung harder each week, from yourself and a friend to a neutral person, someone difficult, then everyone. Rate the warmth 0 to 10 before and after each 15-minute sit.

modalities.name: Precision Absorption Day
modalities.tagline: A strict, teacher-led day of wholehearted effort to steady attention.
modalities.whatItIs: Precision Absorption Day is a proposed one-day intensive in which every block of sitting has an exact object, an exact length and a clear target, all set by a teacher. Do Nothing meditation drops every intention to control attention; this goes to the opposite extreme, asking for wholehearted, precise effort from the first bell to the last. It is meant for people who already have a steady daily practice.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that attention responds to deliberate, precise effort, and one tightly structured day tests how far steady effort can take concentration and warmth.
modalities.whatYouDo: A small group meets with an experienced teacher for six 40-minute sits, each with one assigned target: counting breaths to ten, then holding attention on the breath, then on a warm feeling of goodwill, then letting that feeling absorb attention. Between sits there is short walking and a silent meal, and each time attention slips you note it and begin the count again. The day ends with a short private interview with the teacher.
modalities.whoItsFor: Experienced meditators who want to test and stretch their concentration in a single demanding day rather than on a long retreat.
modalities.cautions: Hours of effortful concentration can bring headaches, strong energy, unusual body sensations or distressing states, so do it only with an experienced teacher and stop if you feel overwhelmed. People with a history of psychosis, mania, dissociation or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first, and this is an untested concept, not a form of therapy.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: the opposite of 'do nothing' meditation. Precision Absorption Day is a teacher-led intensive where every 40-minute sit has an exact target and you give it full, precise effort. For experienced meditators who want to stretch their focus.

modalities.name: The Steady Lamp
modalities.tagline: Hold one warm imagined glow steady, and rest your attention there.
modalities.whatItIs: The Steady Lamp is a concentration idea built on one simple imagined image, the warm glow of a lamp standing for goodwill, which you train yourself to keep stable. If vipassana is about watching every sensation change and pass, this is about steadiness: holding one chosen image unchanged. It is done sitting, almost entirely in the mind, and is usually learned from a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Holding one warm image steady is meant to train calm, stable attention, and it gives goodwill a single place to rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit with eyes closed and picture a small lamp with a soft, warm glow, letting it stand for goodwill toward yourself and others. Each time the image fades, flickers or turns into something else, gently rebuild it as it was, and when it holds steady, let the warmth of the glow fill your attention. Start with 10 minutes and build up to 30 over several weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think in pictures and like a single clear focus, and meditators who want to strengthen steadiness before or alongside insight practice.
modalities.cautions: Straining to hold an image can cause headaches or frustration, so keep the effort light and let the image go when it will not hold. Long imagery-based concentration can produce unusual experiences, so build up slowly, learn longer sits from a teacher and talk to a clinician first if you have a history of psychosis; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Insight meditation watches everything change. This new idea goes the other way: The Steady Lamp. Picture one warm lamp glow standing for goodwill and keep it steady, gently rebuilding it whenever it flickers. Start with 10 minutes.

modalities.name: Remembered Kindnesses
modalities.tagline: Recall times you were cared for, and let the warmth return.
modalities.whatItIs: Remembered Kindnesses is about receiving goodwill rather than producing it: you recall small moments when someone was kind to you and let the warmth of those moments come back. It sits at the far end from high-intensity interval training, with no pushing, no targets and no physical work at all. This proposed practice is done sitting or reclining, alone, in a quiet room.
modalities.coreIdea: Being on the receiving end of kindness can be practiced too, and letting remembered care land is restful rather than effortful.
modalities.whatYouDo: Recline in a comfortable chair for 15 minutes and let a small, specific kindness come to mind, such as a stranger holding a door, a friend's message, or a teacher who believed in you. Picture the moment, notice any warmth or ease it brings, and stay with it without adding phrases or doing anything with it. When the warmth fades, let another small kindness come to mind, or simply rest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired of effort and self-improvement, and those who find giving kindness easier than receiving it.
modalities.cautions: Memories of care can bring grief for people who are gone or a sharp sense of times when kindness was missing, so choose small, recent moments and stop if painful memories take over. If that happens often, a therapist can help; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New idea for anyone tired of trying hard: Remembered Kindnesses. Recline, recall one small time someone was kind to you (a held door, a kind message) and let that warmth return. Nothing to push or produce, just receiving.

modalities.name: Faraway Strangers
modalities.tagline: Alone and still, wish well to people you will never meet.
modalities.whatItIs: Faraway Strangers is a solitary meditation concept that sends goodwill to people you will never meet and who will never know: a nurse on a night shift on another continent, a farmer starting work at dawn. Team sport builds connection through shared play with people right in front of you; this builds it alone, in stillness and entirely in the imagination. It is learned from a teacher, who gives you a sequence to follow.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill needs no contact or reward, and picturing distant strangers can widen your sense of connection even while you are completely alone.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone in a quiet room for 20 minutes and follow the short sequence your teacher has given you, such as six strangers in six different places at this hour. For each one, picture their setting and what they might be doing, then silently wish them well, for example 'may your shift go safely'. End by picturing the whole world at once, half awake and half asleep.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who spend a lot of time on their own, and anyone who wants their goodwill to reach beyond the people they already know.
modalities.cautions: Imagining strangers is not a replacement for real contact, so if loneliness is weighing on you, pair this with reaching out to people or talk to a professional. Picturing hardship can bring sadness, so keep the focus on the wish rather than the suffering; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Concept for quiet evenings alone: Faraway Strangers. Picture a night nurse on another continent, a farmer at dawn, a bus driver on the last route, and silently wish each of them well. Connection without contact, for people who will never know.

modalities.name: Goodwill Pit Stops
modalities.tagline: Many one-minute pauses of goodwill, placed precisely through your day.
modalities.whatItIs: Goodwill Pit Stops breaks loving-kindness into short, scheduled one-minute pauses tied to everyday cues, set up with a teacher. Instead of one long, steady effort, as in endurance exercise, the practice is spread across many brief, precisely placed moments, with no long session at all. A weekly check-in with the teacher adjusts this proposed plan.
modalities.coreIdea: Brief, frequent and well-placed practice can fit into a full day, and planned cues make it easy to remember.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a teacher you choose six to eight daily cues, such as before opening email, while the kettle boils or when sitting down to eat, and a phrase for each. At each cue you stop for one minute, breathe, and silently wish well to whoever is nearest or on your mind. Each week you review with the teacher which cues worked and swap the ones that did not.
modalities.whoItsFor: Busy people who cannot find 20 minutes to sit, and anyone who wants goodwill woven through ordinary moments rather than saved for a cushion.
modalities.cautions: Never use a cue while driving or during any task that needs your full attention. It is an untested idea, and brief pauses are not enough on their own for lasting low mood or anxiety, so seek professional help if those persist.
modalities.tweet: No time to meditate? A new concept: Goodwill Pit Stops. Pick six moments in your day (kettle boiling, opening email, sitting down to eat) and at each one take a single minute to silently wish someone well. Set up with a teacher, tuned weekly.

modalities.name: Gentle With Limits
modalities.tagline: Kindness toward what you cannot do, rather than pushing past it.
modalities.whatItIs: Gentle With Limits is a proposed practice of offering loving-kindness to yourself at the edges of your abilities: tiredness, illness, aging, or a goal you did not reach. Strength training overcomes limits by steadily adding load; this meets them instead, with no load, no target and a softer touch. It is done sitting or lying down, mostly in imagination.
modalities.coreIdea: Limits are part of every life, and meeting them with kindness instead of pressure may make them easier to live with.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or lie comfortably for 15 minutes and picture yourself at a recent moment when you hit a limit, such as being too tired to finish something or needing help with a task. Offer that version of yourself a few wishes, such as 'may I be at ease with what I cannot do today' and 'may I rest without guilt'. Finish by widening the wish to everyone who is meeting a limit right now.
modalities.whoItsFor: People living with tiredness, illness, injury or aging, and high achievers who meet every limit with more pressure.
modalities.cautions: This can bring up grief about health, aging or lost abilities, so go slowly, stop if it deepens into hopelessness and talk to a professional if that feeling persists. It is an untested idea that does not replace medical care or rehabilitation for illness, pain or injury.
modalities.tweet: An untested idea: Gentle With Limits. Instead of pushing past what you can't do, picture yourself at a recent limit (too tired, unwell, older) and wish that self well: 'may I be at ease with what I can't do today.' For anyone who meets limits with pressure.

modalities.name: Whole-Circle Census
modalities.tagline: List everyone in your life, then wish each one well.
modalities.whatItIs: In Whole-Circle Census you write a list of everyone in your life and offer goodwill to a few names each day until no one has been left out. Animal-assisted therapy brings one warm, living companion into the room with a professional team; this untested idea has you work alone, with only a list and your imagination, reaching outward to everyone you know. It is structured and needs no teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill tends to flow to the same few people, and a written census widens it, name by name, to the overlooked, the half-forgotten and the hard to like.
modalities.whatYouDo: Spend one session writing names in three rings: close people, everyday people such as neighbors and coworkers, and distant or difficult people. Each day, sit for 15 minutes, picture the next five names on the list, wish each one well in turn and then tick them off. When the list is done, start again from the top, adding anyone new.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like order and lists, and anyone who notices that their kindness only ever reaches the same handful of people.
modalities.cautions: Names linked to conflict, loss or harm can bring up strong feelings, so you may leave anyone off the list, especially someone who abused or endangered you. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for support with grief or relationship problems.
modalities.tweet: Experimental practice: Whole-Circle Census. Write down everyone in your life (close, everyday and difficult), then each day picture five names and wish each one well. Over the weeks nobody gets skipped, including the people you usually forget.

modalities.name: Glad-for-You Practice
modalities.tagline: Train gladness at other people's good news, in your imagination.
modalities.whatItIs: Glad-for-You Practice is a daily meditation of deliberately rejoicing in other people's good fortune, one of the heart practices traditionally taught alongside loving-kindness. Qigong works through slow, coordinated movement and breath; here the body stays still and all the work happens in the imagination, with a slightly livelier, brighter feel. It is a proposed practice, self-paced and loosely structured.
modalities.coreIdea: Gladness at someone else's good news can be cultivated on purpose, so that other people's success can feel shared rather than lost.
modalities.whatYouDo: During the day, collect two or three bits of good news about other people, such as a friend's new job, a neighbor's thriving garden or a happy reunion you happened to see. In the evening, sit for 10 to 15 minutes, picture each person in their moment of good fortune and let yourself feel glad with them, saying 'I'm glad for you' if it helps. When envy or comparison appears, you notice it kindly and return to someone easier.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who catch themselves comparing or feeling envious, and anyone who wants more everyday sources of gladness.
modalities.cautions: Envy and comparison often show up, especially with people you compete with, so start with people you find it easy to be glad for. It is an untested idea, and if persistent low mood makes gladness feel impossible, talk to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Envy creeping in when friends share good news? A new idea: Glad-for-You Practice. Collect a few bits of other people's good news each day, then in the evening picture each person and let yourself feel glad with them. Start with easy people.

modalities.name: The Unplugged Hour
modalities.tagline: One structured hour of chosen silence, set aside for goodwill.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unplugged Hour is a proposed daily hour of deliberate silence, with no talking, screens or messages, that follows a fixed timetable of goodwill practice. Where socializing seeks open, lively contact with people, this hour is calm and solitary, and the people in your life are held in mind rather than met. A teacher sets the timetable at the start.
modalities.coreIdea: A protected hour without social input gives goodwill a quiet container, so the people in your life are held in mind before you meet them again.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the same time each day, switch off your phone and follow the teacher's plan: 20 minutes of goodwill sitting, 20 minutes of silent household tasks, and 20 more minutes of goodwill sitting. In the sitting blocks you picture the people you will see next and wish each one well. People you live with are told in advance so the silence is respected.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose days are full of talk, messages and calls and who want a dependable daily pause, and those preparing for a silent retreat.
modalities.cautions: Silence can bring loneliness, worry or old memories to the surface, so shorten the hour if it becomes distressing, and do not use it in place of contact if you are already isolated. It is an untested concept and does not replace professional help for anxiety or depression.
modalities.tweet: Proposed: The Unplugged Hour. Phone off for one hour a day: 20 minutes wishing well to the people you'll see next, 20 minutes of quiet chores, 20 more minutes of wishes. A calm, solitary counterweight to days full of talk and messages.

modalities.name: Inner Pilgrimage Route
modalities.tagline: A fixed imagined journey, with a wish at every station.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Pilgrimage Route follows the same scripted, imagined journey every time, stopping at set stations where you meet a person and offer a wish. A walk in nature is open, unplanned and full of real sights and sounds; this guided concept is its indoor opposite, a fixed route through an imagined landscape. A teacher or a recording provides the script.
modalities.coreIdea: A route that never changes becomes familiar, so attention can settle into the wishes rather than into deciding what comes next.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit with eyes closed and follow the same script each time: through a gate, across a bridge, past a market, into a village square and up to a quiet room at the top of a hill. At each station a set person waits (first yourself, then a friend, a stranger, someone difficult and finally everyone), and you stop to offer them a wish before moving on. A session takes about 25 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like stories and guided imagery, and those who find open-ended meditation hard to settle into.
modalities.cautions: Vivid imagery can bring up unexpected feelings or memories, so open your eyes and pause whenever you need to. People with a history of psychosis or dissociation should check with a clinician before regular imagery practice; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: Inner Pilgrimage Route. The same imagined journey every time (a gate, a bridge, a market, a square, a hilltop room), with someone waiting at each stop for your wish. For anyone who finds open-ended meditation hard to settle into.

modalities.name: Low-Light Kindness Sit
modalities.tagline: Turn the senses down so imagined warmth can fill the room.
modalities.whatItIs: Low-Light Kindness Sit is a proposed guided session in a dim, quiet room, where outside sensations are deliberately turned down so that imagined goodwill can take up more of your attention. Sensory mindfulness opens up to everything the senses meet; this does the reverse, quieting the senses and working with imagination instead. Sessions are short and led by a teacher, and the lights can come up at any time.
modalities.coreIdea: With less coming in through the eyes and ears, an imagined feeling of goodwill can become the main thing in awareness.
modalities.whatYouDo: You lie or sit in a dimly lit, quiet room, with an eye mask or earplugs if you like, while a teacher guides a 20-minute session. After a few minutes of settling, you picture people one at a time and offer them wishes, letting the warmth you imagine become vivid and full. The teacher brings the light back up slowly at the end, and you sit for a minute before getting up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are easily distracted by noise and movement, and those who want a more absorbing experience of goodwill than a busy room allows.
modalities.cautions: Low light and quiet can feel disorienting or make some people anxious, especially after trauma or with a fear of the dark or of enclosed spaces, so keep a light within reach and stop whenever you want. People with a history of psychosis or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Prototype idea: Low-Light Kindness Sit. A dim, quiet room and a teacher's voice turn the senses down so that imagined warmth for others can fill your attention. 20 minutes, lights back up slowly at the end, and you can stop whenever you like.

modalities.name: Wishes Sent Ahead
modalities.tagline: Each morning, send a short wish ahead to your future self.
modalities.whatItIs: Wishes Sent Ahead is a morning idea: you picture specific moments coming up in your day or week and send your future self a short wish for each one. Music often stirs memories and is shared with others, whereas this is quiet and solitary and never reaches back into the past. It follows a simple fixed structure and takes about 10 minutes.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill can be aimed forward in time, at the self who will face a hard moment later, instead of back at old memories.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each morning, sit and list three moments ahead of you, such as a difficult call, a long shift or a dentist appointment. Picture yourself in each one, silently send a wish such as 'may you be steady on that call', and then let it go. In the evening you may glance at the list, but there is nothing to grade or review.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who brace themselves for the day ahead, and anyone who wants a brief, structured way to start the morning with kindness toward themselves.
modalities.cautions: Looking ahead can slide into worry or rehearsing problems, so keep each wish short and come back to the present when planning takes over. If anxiety about upcoming events is intense or persistent, talk to a professional; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: Untested concept: Wishes Sent Ahead. Each morning, list three moments coming up (a hard call, a long shift, the dentist), picture yourself there and send a short wish ahead: 'may you be steady.' Ten quiet minutes of kindness aimed at your future self.

modalities.name: Picture-Free Sitting
modalities.tagline: Notice each inner picture fade, and stay with what you sense.
modalities.whatItIs: Picture-Free Sitting is a self-led insight practice that rests on raw sensation and notices every mental picture, memory or story as a passing event. Ideal Parent Figure work deliberately builds rich inner images of caring figures with a therapist; this proposed practice drops the imagery, the past and the guide, leaving just what is actually sensed right now. Anyone can start it alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Seeing images and stories come and go as events, rather than stepping into them, is meant to keep attention in plain present sensation.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 15 to 20 minutes with eyes half open and rest attention on body sensations and sounds. Whenever a picture, memory or story appears, you silently say 'picture', notice it fade and come back to what you can feel and hear. Over time you may notice how often the mind makes pictures, and how quickly they pass when you do not follow them.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds drift into daydreams, replays and imagined scenarios, and meditators who want a simple self-led practice with one clear instruction.
modalities.cautions: Staying with raw sensation can bring up restlessness or anxiety, so keep sits short and eyes open if that happens. Intensive insight meditation can bring difficult experiences, so people with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Invented for daydreamers: Picture-Free Sitting. For 15 minutes, rest on what you can feel and hear. Each time the mind makes a picture, memory or story, silently say 'picture' and watch it fade. One instruction, no teacher needed.

modalities.name: The Undivided Field
modalities.tagline: Feel the whole body at once, as one changing field.
modalities.whatItIs: In The Undivided Field you take in the whole body at once as a single field of tiny, changing sensations, rather than one part or one inner voice at a time. Internal Family Systems divides inner life into parts and talks with each one; this untested concept heads toward an undivided, wordless sense of the whole. It is calm and structured, and it can be learned from a book and practiced alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Experience can be met as one moving whole rather than as many separate pieces, and the practice is meant to train that wide, undivided attention.
modalities.whatYouDo: Begin with a slow sweep of attention from head to feet for five minutes to wake up sensation. Then widen attention to feel the whole body at once, a field of tingling, pressure, warmth and pulsing that is never quite still, and rest there for 15 to 25 minutes. Whenever attention narrows onto one spot or one inner voice, you widen it back out to the whole field.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel pulled in many directions inside, and meditators who want a calm, simple whole-body practice they can do alone.
modalities.cautions: Wide body awareness can sometimes feel strange, as if edges are blurring or you are floating, so open your eyes and feel your feet on the floor if it becomes uncomfortable. People with a history of dissociation, psychosis or severe trauma should talk to a clinician before longer sits; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: One body, one field. The Undivided Field is a new idea: after a short head-to-toe sweep, feel the whole body at once as a single field of tingling, pressure and warmth, and rest there for 20 minutes. For anyone who feels pulled in many directions inside.

modalities.name: Small Discomfort Study
modalities.tagline: Explore an itch or an ache as sensation before reacting.
modalities.whatItIs: Small Discomfort Study is a proposed way of meeting minor, everyday discomforts, such as an itch, a stiff knee or restlessness, by exploring them closely as changing sensations before doing anything about them. Cognitive behavioral therapy works on problems by examining thoughts and changing behavior; this skips both, leaving only close, calm attention to the body. It is self-led and loosely structured.
modalities.coreIdea: Looked at closely, a minor discomfort is a shifting mix of sensations, and the practice is to study it for a while without reacting.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit comfortably for 20 minutes, and when a small discomfort shows up, such as an itch, an ache from sitting or the urge to shift, hold off reacting for a minute or two. During that time you explore it: where exactly it is, whether it burns, presses or tingles, and how it changes from moment to moment. After that you are free to scratch or move, and you notice what the movement feels like too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who react quickly to every small discomfort, and meditators curious about how unpleasant sensations actually behave when they are watched.
modalities.cautions: Use it only with minor, familiar discomforts, never with sharp, new or worsening pain, numbness or other medical symptoms, and move whenever you need to. It is an untested idea and no substitute for medical care for chronic pain.
modalities.tweet: Next time an itch shows up mid-meditation, try this new idea: Small Discomfort Study. Hold off for a minute and explore it. Where is it? Burning or pressing? How does it shift? Then scratch or move if you like. Minor discomforts only.

modalities.name: Body Rhythms Watch
modalities.tagline: Watch the body's own rhythms start and end by themselves.
modalities.whatItIs: Body Rhythms Watch moves through the body's natural rhythms one after another (breath, pulse, swallowing and blinking) and watches each as a cycle that starts and ends on its own. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy works through conversation, metaphors and values-based action, while this proposed practice is wordless and still, with nothing to decide or do. It follows a set order and can be learned from a teacher or a book.
modalities.coreIdea: The body is full of rhythms that rise and fall without your help, and watching them closely shows change happening by itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit still for 25 minutes and spend about five minutes on each rhythm in a set order: the rise and fall of the breath, the pulse felt in the chest or fingertips, the urge and act of swallowing, the blink of the eyes, and finally all of them together. For each one you watch where a cycle begins and where it ends, without speeding it up or slowing it down. If a rhythm is hard to find, you simply rest with the previous one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who prefer quiet bodily practice to talking, and meditators who want a calm, structured way to watch change in the body.
modalities.cautions: Close attention to heartbeat or breathing can make some people anxious, especially with panic attacks or heart worries, so skip those rhythms or switch to sounds if that happens. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for medical advice about heart or breathing symptoms.
modalities.tweet: Your body keeps time all day without you. Body Rhythms Watch, a new idea: sit still and spend five minutes each on breath, pulse, swallowing and blinking, watching each cycle start and end by itself. Quiet, wordless, structured.

modalities.name: Story-Free Feeling
modalities.tagline: Meet emotions as body sensations, without asking why.
modalities.whatItIs: Story-Free Feeling is a self-led idea for meeting emotions purely as sensations in the body, without looking for their causes or meanings. Coherence Therapy works with a therapist to uncover the emotional truth behind a problem; this asks only what is felt, not why, and stays calm and in the present. It suits short daily sits and moments when a feeling shows up during the day.
modalities.coreIdea: An emotion can be met as a set of physical sensations, such as heat, tightness or heaviness, and watched as those sensations shift, without a story attached.
modalities.whatYouDo: When an emotion is present, sit or stand still for 5 to 15 minutes and find where it lives in the body, such as a tight throat, a hot face or a heavy chest. Describe it to yourself only in physical terms (size, temperature, pressure, movement) and watch how it changes. When the mind starts explaining why you feel this way, you note 'story' and come back to the sensation.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to get lost in explaining their feelings, and anyone who wants a simple self-led way to stay with an emotion without being swept away by it.
modalities.cautions: Emotions tied to trauma can be too intense to sit with alone, so stop, ground yourself and seek a trauma-aware therapist if that happens. Some feelings need their causes understood, medical ones included, so this untested idea complements getting help rather than replacing it.
modalities.tweet: Idea: next time a strong feeling shows up, skip the 'why'. Story-Free Feeling means finding it in your body (tight throat, hot face), describing it only as sensation and watching it shift. When explanations start, note 'story' and come back.

modalities.name: Edges of Thought
modalities.tagline: Catch the exact moment each thought begins and ends.
modalities.whatItIs: Edges of Thought is a proposed insight meditation that takes thinking itself as its object, watching closely for the moment each thought begins and the moment it dissolves. In tension and trauma releasing exercises the body leads and shakes; here the body stays still and attention turns to the mind. It is calm and structured, and it is usually learned from a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Thoughts are events with edges, and noticing where they start and stop, rather than what they say, shows how quickly they come and go.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes and wait, alert but relaxed, for the next thought to appear, the way a cat waits by a mouse hole. When one appears, note 'start' without following its content, and then note 'gone' when it fades or turns into another thought. Between thoughts, rest in whatever quiet or sensation is there until the next one arrives.
modalities.whoItsFor: People caught up in busy thinking who are curious about how thoughts actually behave, and meditators who want to add the mind to body-based insight practice.
modalities.cautions: Watching thoughts closely can at first make them seem louder or faster, so shorten the sit or switch to sounds if it feels agitating. If intrusive or distressing thoughts dominate, talk with a professional, and people with a history of psychosis should check with a clinician first; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Can you catch a thought starting? Edges of Thought is a new concept: sit still and wait for the next thought like a cat at a mouse hole. Note 'start' when it appears and 'gone' when it fades, without following what it says.

modalities.name: Coin-Sized Sweep
modalities.tagline: Move attention through the body one small patch at a time.
modalities.whatItIs: Coin-Sized Sweep moves attention through the whole body in small, coin-sized patches, in a strict order and at a steady pace. Focusing waits openly at one vague bodily sense until words or meaning arise; this proposed method covers every patch systematically and notices only physical qualities, never meaning. It is usually learned from a teacher and then practiced alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Systematic, fine-grained attention reveals how much is happening in every part of the body, and how none of it stays the same.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit still and start at the crown of the head, resting on a coin-sized patch for one or two breaths, then moving to the next patch along a set route down the face, neck, arms, torso and legs to the toes. In each patch you notice only physical qualities, such as pressure, warmth, tingling or nothing at all, and move on even if nothing is felt. One full pass takes 30 to 45 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: Detail-minded people who like a clear method, and meditators who find open-ended attention to the body too vague.
modalities.cautions: Long sweeps can bring numbness, strong tingling, emotions or memories, so take breaks and keep passes shorter at first. People with a history of trauma, dissociation or psychosis should start with short sessions and talk to a clinician before intensive practice; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Detail lovers, here's a new idea: Coin-Sized Sweep. Move attention through your body one coin-sized patch at a time, crown to toes, a breath or two each, noticing only pressure, warmth or tingling. No meanings, just a methodical tour.

modalities.name: Clicker Tally Log
modalities.tagline: Count what passes through your mind, and log it.
modalities.whatItIs: Clicker Tally Log is an untested self-run insight practice in which you count each experience you notice by type, using a small hand clicker or tally marks, and log the totals after every sit. Aletheia Coaching lets experience unfold openly with a coach; this is its rigid, measurable, do-it-yourself opposite. It turns the flow of experience into numbers you can look back on.
modalities.coreIdea: Counting what arises (thinking, hearing, feeling) makes the constant flow of experience concrete and visible, and is meant to keep attention alert.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes holding a hand clicker and click once each time you clearly notice a thought arise; in later weeks you can track sounds or body sensations on a second counter. After the sit, write the totals and one sentence about what you noticed in a notebook. Every few weeks, look back over the numbers for patterns, such as busier mornings or quieter evenings.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like data and self-tracking, and meditators who want a concrete, self-run way to stay alert during a sit.
modalities.cautions: Counting can turn into scorekeeping or self-judgment, so regard high and low numbers as equally interesting and drop the clicker if it becomes a source of stress. It is an untested idea, and if tracking starts to feed checking or worry, stop.
modalities.tweet: Meditation, but with a clicker. Clicker Tally Log, a new concept: click once each time you notice a thought arise, log the total after a 20-minute sit, and look for patterns over the weeks. Self-run and very data-friendly.

modalities.name: Metronome Labeling Drill
modalities.tagline: Name what you notice, once a second, with a teacher.
modalities.whatItIs: Metronome Labeling Drill is a proposed teacher-led insight drill in which you silently name the most obvious experience at a steady, set pace of about once a second, sometimes to a soft metronome. Do Nothing meditation drops all technique and control; this goes to the opposite extreme, with maximum method, pace and precision. It runs in short sets, with a teacher checking in between them.
modalities.coreIdea: The idea is that a fast, regular rhythm of noticing leaves little room for drifting and shows how quickly experience changes.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a small, silent group, you sit for sets of 10 minutes and, at each soft tick, silently label whatever is most obvious right then, such as 'hearing', 'pressure', 'thinking' or 'tingling'. Between sets you take a short walking break and briefly tell the teacher how the pace felt, and the teacher speeds it up, slows it down or simplifies the labels. A session lasts about an hour.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators whose minds drift a lot in open sitting, and people who like drills and clear rules.
modalities.cautions: Fast, intensive labeling can bring strong energy, anxiety or unsettling changes in perception, particularly on retreat, so practice it only with an experienced teacher and slow down whenever it feels like too much. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Novel drill for drifting minds: Metronome Labeling Drill. At each soft tick, silently name what's most obvious ('hearing', 'pressure', 'thinking'), in 10-minute sets, with a teacher adjusting the pace. Maximum method, minimum drifting.

modalities.name: Even-Handed Sensing
modalities.tagline: Give neutral sensations the same interest as pleasant ones.
modalities.whatItIs: Even-Handed Sensing turns attention toward the neutral sensations we usually ignore, such as the touch of clothing or the stillness of the hands, and gives pleasant, unpleasant and neutral sensations exactly the same plain interest. Loving-kindness and absorption practice deliberately build a pleasant feeling; this proposed practice cultivates nothing and prefers nothing. It is calm and bodily, and it can be learned from a book or a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Attention usually chases the pleasant and fights the unpleasant, and the practice is to meet all three kinds of sensation with the same even interest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes, find a neutral sensation, such as the contact of a sleeve, the weight of the hands or the middle of the back, and rest attention there. When a pleasant or unpleasant sensation pulls at you, silently note 'pleasant' or 'unpleasant', give it the same plain attention for a few breaths, and then return to a neutral spot. Over time you notice how attention leans toward some sensations and away from others.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who notice that they chase pleasant states or battle unpleasant ones, and anyone curious about the quiet, overlooked parts of experience.
modalities.cautions: Neutral sensations can feel boring, drowsy or flat, and with low mood that flatness can feel heavier, so keep sits short and alternate them with activity. Intensive practice can bring difficult experiences, and people with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: The overlooked sensations get their turn. Even-Handed Sensing, an untested idea, rests on the neutral ones (a sleeve's touch, the weight of your hands). When something pleasant or unpleasant pulls, give it the same plain interest, then return. #mindfulness

modalities.name: Mood Weather Watch
modalities.tagline: Watch your mood shift like weather, without trying to change it.
modalities.whatItIs: Mood Weather Watch is an insight idea that takes your overall mood, the background emotional weather, as its object and watches it shift on its own, without trying to lift or lower it. High-intensity interval training changes your state through maximal effort; this asks for no effort, no target and very little structure, just calm watching. A teacher introduces it, and then you practice alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Moods, like weather, keep changing by themselves, and the practice is simply to watch that happen without pushing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or recline for 15 minutes and, every minute or so, silently name the weather inside, such as 'gray', 'bright', 'stormy' or 'still'. You do not try to improve the mood or find its cause; you only notice how it shifts, even slightly, over the session. On some days you add three brief check-ins (morning, afternoon and evening) and notice how the weather has changed in between.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel run by their moods, and anyone who is tired of effortful self-improvement and wants a gentle way to watch rather than manage.
modalities.cautions: If low mood is persistent, severe or comes with thoughts of self-harm, watching it is not enough: talk to a doctor or mental health professional promptly. It is an untested idea and does not replace care for depression or anxiety.
modalities.tweet: Gray, bright, stormy, still. Mood Weather Watch is a proposed practice: every minute or so, silently name the weather inside and simply watch it change, without trying to improve it. 15 minutes, no effort. For anyone who feels run by their moods.

modalities.name: Crowded Empty Room
modalities.tagline: Alone in a room, notice how often the mind brings people in.
modalities.whatItIs: Crowded Empty Room is a proposed insight practice done in complete solitude that watches how often the mind fills an empty room with other people: imagined conversations, replayed chats, planned replies. Team sport is built on playing with and against others; here you are entirely alone and still, and the social mind itself becomes the object. It is learned from a teacher who checks in now and then.
modalities.coreIdea: Even alone, the mind stays busy with other people, and seeing that clearly, without joining the conversations, is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone in a quiet room for 25 minutes and rest attention on the sensations of sitting. Each time the mind brings someone in (a conversation, a face, a reply you are drafting), you silently note 'people', notice how it feels in the body and return to sitting. Every couple of weeks you tell your teacher what you noticed, such as which people visit most often.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who replay conversations or rehearse what they will say, and meditators curious about the social side of the mind.
modalities.cautions: Replayed conversations can stir loneliness, resentment or rumination, so shorten the sit or switch to sounds if it gets heavy. Solitary practice is not a replacement for real contact if you are isolated or lonely; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Alone in a room, how many people are in your head? A new idea, Crowded Empty Room: 25 minutes of solitude, and each time an imagined conversation or replayed chat shows up, note 'people' and come back to sitting. For anyone who replays old chats.

modalities.name: Random Bell Snapshots
modalities.tagline: Random bells through the day, thirty seconds of noticing each time.
modalities.whatItIs: Random Bell Snapshots is a daily-life insight idea: bells ring at random times and, at each one, you pause for 30 seconds to notice what is present. Endurance training is one long, continuous effort, whereas this is many brief, unpredictable snapshots, set up and reviewed with a teacher. It needs only a phone app that can ring at random.
modalities.coreIdea: Many short, random moments of noticing give a picture of how experience actually changes across a whole day, not just on a cushion.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a teacher you set an app to ring six to ten times a day at random between set hours, with quiet hours for sleep, meetings and driving. At each bell you stop for 30 seconds and silently note what is there, such as seeing, hearing, thinking, tension or ease, then jot one word in a log. Each week you review the log with your teacher and adjust the number of bells.
modalities.whoItsFor: Busy people who cannot sit for long, and meditators who want insight practice to reach into ordinary moments.
modalities.cautions: Turn the bells off while driving, cycling or doing anything else that needs full attention. If the bells start to feel stressful, reduce them; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Your phone chimes at random, six to ten times a day. Each time, stop for 30 seconds and notice what's there (seeing, hearing, thinking, tension), then log one word. Random Bell Snapshots, an untested idea for people who can't sit for long. 🔔

modalities.name: Ownerless Moments
modalities.tagline: Notice how much happens on its own, without a doer.
modalities.whatItIs: Ownerless Moments is a proposed teacher-guided insight practice that notices how much of experience simply happens: sounds arrive, thoughts appear and the breath goes on, with no one making them happen. Strength training builds a strong sense of 'I can' through effort against a load; this explores, calmly and without effort, experience that has no doer. It is one of the more unusual ideas on this map and needs a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Much of experience seems to arrive by itself, and this practice explores that directly, without effort or control.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes and let attention rest on whatever is most obvious. Instead of thinking 'I hear' or 'I am breathing', you silently note 'hearing happens', 'breathing happens' or 'thinking happens', and notice whether any controller can actually be found. The teacher meets you weekly to talk through what you noticed and to adjust or pause the practice.
modalities.whoItsFor: Experienced meditators curious about the Buddhist idea of not-self, and people who feel worn out by always having to be in control.
modalities.cautions: This can feel unsettling, as if things are unreal or you are detached from yourself, so stop, open your eyes, move and talk to someone if that happens. People with a history of dissociation, depersonalization or psychosis should avoid it unless a clinician agrees; it is an untested concept and needs an experienced teacher.
modalities.tweet: Who is doing the hearing? Ownerless Moments is a teacher-guided concept: note 'hearing happens' and 'thinking happens', and check whether any controller can be found. Calm and effortless, but not for everyone, so do it with a teacher.

modalities.name: Contact Rounds
modalities.tagline: Rounds of attention through everywhere your body touches something.
modalities.whatItIs: Contact Rounds moves attention in rounds through every place where the body is touching something: floor, chair, clothing and your own resting hands. Animal-assisted therapy offers the touch and presence of a living companion with a professional team; this proposed practice explores touch alone and self-led, with no one else there. It follows a fixed order and is easy to learn from a short guide.
modalities.coreIdea: Touch is always happening, and moving through every point of contact in turn shows each one as a changing stream of pressure, warmth and texture.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone for 20 minutes and move attention in a fixed round: feet on the floor, seat on the chair, back against the chair, hands resting on each other, clothes on the shoulders, air on the face. Stay with each contact for three breaths, noticing pressure, temperature and texture and how they shift, then move on. Repeat the round, a little more slowly each time.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a simple, concrete practice they can do anywhere on their own, and meditators who find the breath too subtle to follow.
modalities.cautions: Attention to touch can sometimes bring up memories or discomfort, especially after trauma, so keep your eyes open and skip any contact point that feels unsafe. Intensive practice can bring difficult experiences, so people with a history of psychosis or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Small new practice: Contact Rounds. Move attention through every place you're touching something (feet on floor, seat on chair, hands on each other) for three breaths each, noticing pressure and warmth shift. Alone, anywhere, no gear.

modalities.name: Intention Spotting
modalities.tagline: Notice the tiny intention that comes before every small movement.
modalities.whatItIs: Intention Spotting is an untested insight practice that watches for the faint intention that appears just before each small action, such as swallowing, shifting or opening the eyes. Qigong coordinates slow movement and breath with a focused mind; this guides nothing and simply watches intentions themselves appear and fade. It is calm and mostly about the mind, with the body kept still.
modalities.coreIdea: Many small actions seem to be preceded by a faint intention, and noticing it shows how choices arise moment by moment.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 20 minutes and let the body be still but not rigid. When you feel the impulse to swallow, scratch, shift or open your eyes, you note 'intending' and watch the intention for a moment before letting the action happen or not, whichever comes naturally. Later you can try it while sipping tea or standing up, noticing the intention before each small movement.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they act on autopilot, and meditators curious about how choices form.
modalities.cautions: Close attention to small movements can feel awkward or make some people self-conscious, so keep it light and stop if it brings tension. Intensive practice can bring difficult experiences, and people with a history of psychosis or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Before you swallow, shift or blink, there's a tiny intention. Intention Spotting, a novel practice: sit still, note 'intending' when one appears, watch it a moment, then let the movement happen or not. For anyone who feels on autopilot.

modalities.name: Silent Home Timetable
modalities.tagline: One silent day at home, every hour planned, no contact.
modalities.whatItIs: Silent Home Timetable is a proposed one-day home retreat in complete silence, with no talking, screens or messages, following an hour-by-hour timetable written by a teacher. Socializing is about open, lively contact; this is a day of solitude, with every hour structured around body-focused insight practice. A teacher phones at the start and the end of the day.
modalities.coreIdea: Removing all social input for one structured day leaves the body and mind as the only things to watch.
modalities.whatYouDo: The timetable alternates 45-minute sits, in which you slowly sweep attention through the body, with slow walking indoors, a silent mindful lunch and a rest period. Housemates are told in advance, the phone stays off except for the teacher's two calls, and the day runs from about 7 in the morning to 7 in the evening. You end by writing a few lines about the day before turning your phone back on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People curious about retreats who cannot travel to one, and meditators who want a day of deep practice without leaving home.
modalities.cautions: A full day of silence and sitting can bring up hard experiences such as fear, panic or old memories, so keep the teacher's number handy and end the day early if you feel overwhelmed. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma, or anyone in a current crisis, should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Can't get away for a retreat? Concept: Silent Home Timetable. One day at home, phone off, no talking, every hour planned by a teacher: sits, slow walking, a silent lunch, rest. The teacher calls at the start and end.

modalities.name: Fixed Chair, Moving Mind
modalities.tagline: Same chair, same time, same method, never the same experience.
modalities.whatItIs: Fixed Chair, Moving Mind is a daily insight practice in which the setting never changes: the same chair, the same time and the same 30-minute method set by a teacher. A nature walk is open, wandering and different every time; this proposed practice stays indoors and fixed, so that the only thing that varies is experience itself. It is highly structured and meant to run for months.
modalities.coreIdea: When everything outside is held constant, it becomes obvious that inner experience is never the same twice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each day, at the same time, sit in the same chair in the same room and follow the same sequence: 10 minutes on the breath, 15 minutes sweeping attention through the body and five minutes on sounds. Afterwards, write one sentence about what was different from yesterday. Once a month, review the sentences with your teacher.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like routine, and meditators who want a steady, long-term practice that makes change easy to see.
modalities.cautions: Rigid routines can turn into a source of stress, so if a missed day brings strong guilt, loosen the rules. It is an untested idea, and people with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe trauma should talk to a clinician before deepening any meditation practice.
modalities.tweet: Same chair, same time, same method, every day for months. Fixed Chair, Moving Mind is an untested idea built on that: with the setting fixed, the only thing left to vary is your experience. One sentence a day on what was different.

modalities.name: Three-Line Insight Journal
modalities.tagline: Three short written lines after each sit, reviewed with a teacher.
modalities.whatItIs: Three-Line Insight Journal pairs structured sitting with a brief written reflection on three classic themes of insight meditation, put into plain words: change, dissatisfaction and the absence of a fixed self. Sensory mindfulness stays with plain sensing, while this proposed practice adds reflection, words and a teacher's guidance. It suits people who make sense of experience by writing.
modalities.coreIdea: Writing a few plain lines after each sit can turn fleeting observations into a clearer understanding over the weeks.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 20-minute sit, write three lines: one thing you saw change, one moment when something did not satisfy or you wanted more, and one thing that happened by itself without you doing it. Keep the lines short and descriptive rather than analytical. Every two weeks, read the journal through with a teacher, who helps you notice patterns.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think best on paper, and meditators who want guidance in making sense of what they notice.
modalities.cautions: Reflection can slide into rumination or harsh self-judgment, so keep each line short and factual and skip the writing on days it feels heavy. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for therapy if hard material keeps coming up.
modalities.tweet: For meditators who think on paper, a proposed habit: the Three-Line Insight Journal. After each sit, write one thing that changed, one moment of wanting more, and one thing that happened by itself. Review it with a teacher every two weeks.

modalities.name: Listening for Silence
modalities.tagline: Listen to the silence itself, and let sounds come and go.
modalities.whatItIs: Listening for Silence is a solitary insight idea that takes the quiet itself as its object, letting sounds appear and vanish against it like visitors. Music fills silence with melody, rhythm and feeling and is often shared; this is done alone, with no music and no meaning, only everyday sounds and the silence around them. It is calm, structured and stays in the present.
modalities.coreIdea: Silence is always there between and beneath sounds, and resting in it shows every sound as something that begins, lasts a moment and ends.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone in a quiet room for 20 minutes with eyes closed, and for the first few minutes simply listen to whatever sounds are there, such as a distant car, a fridge hum or your own breath. Then shift attention to the silence around and between them, noting 'sound' when one arrives and 'silence' when it has gone. In the last five minutes, rest in the quiet itself and let any sound pass through without following it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who love listening or feel crowded by constant noise, and anyone who wants a quiet, simple insight practice without music or spoken guidance.
modalities.cautions: In very quiet rooms, ringing in the ears (tinnitus) or sound sensitivity can become more noticeable or distressing, so stop or add gentle background sound if that happens. Intensive practice can bring difficult experiences, and people with a history of psychosis or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first; as a new idea, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: No music, no voice, just the quiet underneath. Listening for Silence is a new idea: 20 minutes alone, letting each sound arrive and fade while your attention rests on the silence it came from. For anyone who feels crowded by noise.

modalities.name: Landmark Hill Repeats
modalities.tagline: A real hill sets the effort, and you need no one else.
modalities.whatItIs: Landmark Hill Repeats is a proposed self-led interval session on a real hill, where the slope sets the effort and the walk back down sets the rest, so nothing is needed beyond a fixed number of climbs. Ideal Parent Figure work relies on a therapist and imagined supportive figures; this relies on no one, stays in the present and is grounded in what you actually see and feel. It keeps the hard, structured core of interval training.
modalities.coreIdea: The landscape can be the whole protocol: a fixed hill and a fixed landmark make the session simple, honest and entirely your own.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute easy warm-up, run or climb briskly up a steep hill to a chosen landmark, such as a tree or a lamp post, at hard effort, then walk slowly back down as recovery. Repeat four to eight times, keeping the same landmark every session, and take in what you see and hear at the top before turning around. Finish with 10 minutes of easy walking.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want hard exercise without gadgets, classes or coaches, and anyone who likes being outdoors and relying on themselves.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting, high blood pressure or another serious condition, and build a base of easier exercise before hard hill efforts. Choose a safe hill with good footing and light, stop at chest pain or dizziness, and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: No app, no coach, no gadgets: just a hill. Landmark Hill Repeats, an untested concept: climb hard to the same tree or lamp post, walk down slowly to recover, repeat four to eight times. The landscape is the whole plan.

modalities.name: The Signed Card
modalities.tagline: Decide the whole session in advance, then simply follow it.
modalities.whatItIs: The Signed Card is a self-led interval idea: you write the exact session on a card the night before, including firm safety stop rules, sign it and follow it to the letter. Internal Family Systems listens to many inner voices and negotiates with each one; here one decision is made in advance, so no inner bargaining happens during the effort. It is fully structured and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Deciding once, calmly and in advance, is meant to take the bargaining out of the hard moments, while pre-written safety rules keep your body's real warning signs in charge.
modalities.whatYouDo: The evening before, write the session on a card, for example a 10-minute warm-up, six 1-minute hard bouts on a bike with 2 minutes easy between, and a cool-down, plus stop rules such as chest pain, dizziness or sharp joint pain. Sign it and leave it where you will see it. During the session, thoughts like 'skip the last one' are noticed and let go, and only the stop rules can change the plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who often talk themselves out of workouts halfway through, and anyone who likes the clarity of a commitment made in advance.
modalities.cautions: The stop rules always beat the card: halt at chest pain, dizziness, faintness or sharp pain, and get medical advice before hard exercise if you have heart disease, high blood pressure or another serious condition. Build up gradually with easy days between sessions; the concept itself is untested.
modalities.tweet: Ever bargain with yourself mid-workout? The Signed Card, a new idea: write tomorrow's interval session on a card tonight, with firm stop rules for pain or dizziness, sign it, then follow it exactly. Decide once, not every minute.

modalities.name: Quiet-Mind Bouts
modalities.tagline: Let hard effort crowd out thinking, then notice the quiet.
modalities.whatItIs: Quiet-Mind Bouts is a proposed interval practice that uses hard bouts as a deliberate break from thinking: attention goes entirely to the raw sensations of effort, and recovery is spent noticing how quiet the mind has become. Cognitive behavioral therapy works on thoughts by examining and questioning them; this sets thinking aside by flooding attention with sensation. There is no self-talk, no analysis and no scorekeeping.
modalities.coreIdea: During very hard effort many people find little room left for thinking, and the session uses that on purpose as a short, physical holiday from the mind.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike, a rower or a track, do six to eight hard bouts of 30 to 60 seconds, and during each one put all your attention on the burning legs, the heavy breathing and the pounding heart. During each two-minute easy recovery, notice how quiet or busy the mind is, without judging it. Cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who overthink and want a physical break from their own thoughts, and anyone who finds sitting meditation too hard to settle into.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart problems, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, build a base before hard bouts and stop at chest pain or dizziness. It is an untested idea that does not replace care for anxiety or persistent worry, so seek help if worry or low mood lasts.
modalities.tweet: Hard effort can leave little room for thinking. Quiet-Mind Bouts is a speculative practice that uses this on purpose: put all attention on burning legs and heavy breath during each bout, then notice how quiet your mind is while you recover.

modalities.name: Inch-Up Scoreboard
modalities.tagline: One number per session, nudged up in tiny steps.
modalities.whatItIs: Inch-Up Scoreboard is a self-run interval program built around a single measured score per session, such as meters rowed in each 30-second bout, which you aim to nudge up by tiny amounts over weeks. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy makes room for difficult feelings and steers by personal values; this untested concept steers entirely by a number and aims straight at changing the body. It is fully structured and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: A visible score that creeps upward makes progress concrete, as long as the steps stay tiny and a bad day counts as data rather than failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: Warm up for 10 minutes on a rowing machine, then row eight 30-second hard bouts with 90 seconds easy between, noting the meters for each bout. Write the average on a scoreboard on your wall, and next session aim to beat it by one or two meters at most, or simply match it. Every fourth week is an easier week with no target.
modalities.whoItsFor: People motivated by numbers and visible progress, and anyone who wants proof on paper that their training is going somewhere.
modalities.cautions: Chasing a number can push you into overreaching, injury or poor form, so keep the steps tiny, take the easy weeks and stop a bout if your technique breaks down. Get medical advice first if you have heart, blood pressure or back problems, and stop at chest pain or dizziness; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: For the number-motivated: Inch-Up Scoreboard, a new concept. Eight hard 30-second rows, average meters on a scoreboard, then try to beat it by a meter or two next time. Tiny steps, an easy week every fourth week, progress you can see.

modalities.name: Let the Pulse Decide
modalities.tagline: Your pulse, not the clock, decides when the next bout starts.
modalities.whatItIs: In Let the Pulse Decide, each rest lasts exactly as long as your heart needs: the next hard bout starts only when your pulse falls back to a set number. Coherence Therapy looks for the hidden emotional meaning behind a problem with a therapist; this proposed session has no meaning or story, just the body's own present-moment signal deciding what happens next. It is self-led and needs only a watch or a heart rate monitor.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting recovery, not a fixed timer, set the rest keeps each session matched to how your body is doing that day.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before starting, pick a recovery pulse, such as the heart rate you have during brisk walking.
