After a 10-minute warm-up, do a 1-minute hard bout on a bike or on foot, then move easily until your pulse, counted at the wrist for 10 seconds or read from a monitor, falls to that number, and only then start the next bout. Stop after six to eight bouts, or sooner if recovery starts taking twice as long as it did at the beginning.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like listening to their bodies, and anyone whose energy varies a lot from day to day and who wants sessions that adjust by themselves.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, an irregular heartbeat, chest pain or fainting, or take medicines that affect heart rate, since these can make pulse targets misleading. Wrist monitors can be inaccurate during hard effort, so also go by how you feel, stop at chest pain or dizziness and keep easy days between sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Experimental twist on intervals: Let the Pulse Decide. After each hard minute, recover until your pulse drops back to a set number, and only then go again. Your heart sets the rest, not the clock, so each session fits the day you're having.

modalities.name: Exact-Split Repeats
modalities.tagline: Hit a target time to the second, again and again.
modalities.whatItIs: Exact-Split Repeats is an interval idea in which the goal is control rather than top speed: you run or row a fixed distance again and again, aiming to hit a target time within one second each time, while a partner calls out your times. Tension and trauma releasing exercises let the body shake on its own; here every movement is voluntary, precise and deliberately steered. The effort stays hard but measured.
modalities.coreIdea: Commanding your pace precisely while working hard is practice in deliberate control of the body, instead of letting it run away with you.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, run 200 meters on a track or row 250 meters, aiming for a target time that feels hard but repeatable, such as 50 seconds, with 90 seconds of walking or easy rowing between. A partner calls each time, and you adjust your pace to land within one second of the target. Do six to ten repeats and finish with an easy cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy precision and skill, and those who tend to start too fast and fade, who want to learn steady control under effort.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart problems, high blood pressure or another serious condition, and build up slowly to avoid strains, especially in the calves and hamstrings. Keep targets hard but not all-out, stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain, and rest between hard days; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Not faster, more exact. Exact-Split Repeats is a new idea: run 200 m (or row 250 m) again and again, trying to hit the same target time within one second while a partner calls it out. Hard effort, total control.

modalities.name: Flat-Out Strides
modalities.tagline: Very short bursts of pure speed, with full rest between.
modalities.whatItIs: Flat-Out Strides is a proposed interval session made of very short bursts at the fastest speed you can hold with good form, each followed by full recovery. Focusing slows right down and waits patiently for a vague bodily sense to become clear; this is about immediacy, quickness and decisive action. The aim is speed itself, not exhaustion.
modalities.coreIdea: Pure quickness, practiced in tiny doses with long rests, offers an intense, clean experience of speed without grinding fatigue.
modalities.whatYouDo: On a flat grass field or a track, warm up for 15 minutes with jogging and gradually faster practice runs. Then run six to eight bursts of 8 to 12 seconds, accelerating smoothly to top speed, each followed by one to two minutes of walking until you feel fully recovered. Stop the session as soon as your speed or form starts to drop.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find long hard intervals miserable but enjoy short bursts of speed, and anyone who wants to feel quick and light again.
modalities.cautions: Sprinting can strain hamstrings and calves, so warm up thoroughly, stay at about three quarters of full speed for the first few weeks and build up gradually. Get medical advice first if you have heart, blood pressure or joint problems, and stop at chest pain, dizziness or any sharp pull; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: Hate long, grinding intervals? Try this idea: Flat-Out Strides. Eight to twelve seconds of pure speed on grass, then walk until fully recovered. Six to eight bursts, stopping as soon as your form fades. Quick, clean, done.

modalities.name: The Unchanging Four
modalities.tagline: One fixed session, repeated for months, as a yardstick for change.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unchanging Four is a self-run interval routine in which one session, four hard 4-minute bouts with 3 easy minutes between, is repeated twice a week for months without ever changing. Aletheia Coaching lets each conversation unfold openly with a coach; this untested concept is a fixed, closed protocol that you run entirely by yourself. What changes is not the plan but how it feels and what your body can do.
modalities.coreIdea: When the session never changes, it becomes a fixed yardstick, and changes in effort, breathing and recovery become easy to see.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week, on the same bike or the same route, warm up for 10 minutes, then do four 4-minute bouts at hard effort, breathing heavily and barely able to talk, with 3 minutes of easy movement between. Cool down for 5 to 10 minutes and write one line on how it felt and, if you track it, your heart rate. Never change the protocol; on bad days, simply ease the effort.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like routine and want a simple, long-term plan with no decisions to make, and anyone curious to see their own fitness change against a fixed benchmark.
modalities.cautions: Four-minute hard bouts put real strain on the heart, so get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build a base of easier exercise before starting. Repetition can lead to overuse niggles or boredom, so take extra rest when needed and stop at chest pain or dizziness; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Four hard 4-minute bouts with 3 easy minutes between, twice a week, for months, never changed. The Unchanging Four is an untested concept: the plan stays still, so the only thing left to change is you.

modalities.name: Work-and-Watch Pairs
modalities.tagline: Two people, one machine: your rest is your partner's work.
modalities.whatItIs: Work-and-Watch Pairs is a proposed partner workout in which two people share one bike, rower or stretch of track and take turns: while one works hard, the other recovers, times them and watches their form, then they swap. Do Nothing meditation drops all effort and control; this goes to the opposite extreme, a session where there is always something to do and someone counting on you. It is fully structured and best learned from a coach or a class first.
modalities.coreIdea: Shared, continuous doing, with rest and effort passing back and forth between partners, is meant to keep both people engaged and accountable.
modalities.whatYouDo: After warming up together, partner A does a 45-second hard bout while partner B recovers, calls the time and watches A's form, then B works while A recovers, for eight to ten rounds each. Partners agree beforehand on their own target efforts, so neither is racing the other. You finish with a shared cool-down and a quick word about how it went.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who skip workouts when alone, friends or couples who want to train together, and anyone who likes having a role at every moment.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, high blood pressure or another serious condition, and keep partner sessions cooperative rather than competitive, since racing each other raises the risk of overdoing it. Stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain, and rest between hard days; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: Two people, one rower, no idle moments. Work-and-Watch Pairs is a proposed workout: while you go hard for 45 seconds, your partner rests, calls the time and watches your form, then you swap. Eight to ten rounds each, cooperative, not a race.

modalities.name: Whistle-Start Sprints
modalities.tagline: Every burst starts on a signal you cannot predict.
modalities.whatItIs: Whistle-Start Sprints is an interval idea in which each hard bout starts on an unpredictable outside signal, such as a partner's whistle, a clap or an app with random delays, so attention stays outward and alert. Loving-kindness and absorption meditation turn attention inward to imagined people and warm feelings; this turns it outward, toward sharp, real-time perception. It is done with a partner or in a small group.
modalities.coreIdea: Waiting for a signal you cannot predict pulls attention outward into the present moment, ready to move.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, stand ready at a start line while a partner waits a random 3 to 15 seconds before blowing a whistle. On the whistle you sprint, or pedal hard on a bike, for 10 to 20 seconds, then walk back and recover for about a minute and a half before the next round. Do six to ten rounds, swapping roles if your partner is training too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who drift off during workouts, those who enjoy games and reaction challenges, and anyone who wants exercise that wakes up their attention.
modalities.cautions: Sudden explosive starts can strain muscles, so warm up well, begin at moderate speed and build up over weeks, and get medical advice first if you have heart, blood pressure or joint problems. Use a flat, clear area, stop at chest pain or dizziness and rest between hard days; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: On your marks, then wait. In Whistle-Start Sprints, a new concept, a partner waits a random 3 to 15 seconds before whistling, and you sprint for 10 to 20 seconds. Walk back, recover, repeat six to ten times. Exercise that keeps attention sharp and outward.

modalities.name: Three-Gear Shifts
modalities.tagline: Practice shifting your state on command: easy, hard, flat-out.
modalities.whatItIs: Three-Gear Shifts is a proposed continuous interval session built around three gears (easy, hard and flat-out) that you switch between on a fixed schedule. Vipassana watches experience change by itself without reacting; this changes your own state on purpose, again and again. It can be done alone with a timer or with a partner calling the gears.
modalities.coreIdea: Shifting up and down on command, many times in one session, practices a deliberate kind of control over how activated you are.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up on a bike or a rower, work through a 3-minute block of 90 seconds easy, 60 seconds hard and 30 seconds flat-out, then repeat the block five or six times without stopping. The skill is in the transitions: hitting each new gear quickly and cleanly, and especially dropping back to easy right away. Finish with a 10-minute cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to switch on or to switch off, and anyone who wants a workout that trains control rather than just endurance.
modalities.cautions: Flat-out efforts strain the heart and muscles, so get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build up with the easy and hard gears before adding flat-out. Stop at chest pain or dizziness and keep easy days between sessions; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Easy, hard, flat-out, repeat. Three-Gear Shifts is a new idea: 90 seconds easy, 60 hard and 30 flat-out, five or six times without stopping. The skill is in the shifts, especially dropping back to easy fast. #HIIT

modalities.name: Empty Stairwell Sessions
modalities.tagline: Hard stair climbs, entirely alone, with no audience or comparison.
modalities.whatItIs: Empty Stairwell Sessions is a solitary interval idea for a quiet staircase, with no audience, no leaderboard and nothing shared online. Team sport thrives on playing with and against others, while this keeps effort private, uncompared and turned inward. It is fully structured but needs no gym, class or partner.
modalities.coreIdea: Effort with no one watching and no one to beat belongs entirely to you, free of comparison and performance.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up of easy stair walking, climb a set number of flights, such as four, briskly and hard, then walk down slowly holding the rail as your recovery. Repeat six to ten times, and keep no record except a single tick on a private calendar. Finish with easy walking and stretching.
modalities.whoItsFor: People put off by gyms, group classes or fitness apps that compare and share, and anyone who wants hard exercise to be a private matter.
modalities.cautions: Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and because you are alone, carry a phone and tell someone where you are. Use a well-lit stairwell, always walk down slowly with a hand on the rail, and stop at chest pain or dizziness; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: No leaderboard, no class, no one watching. Empty Stairwell Sessions is a new concept: climb four flights hard, walk down slowly holding the rail, repeat six to ten times. Effort that's private and compared with no one.

modalities.name: Scattered Hard Minutes
modalities.tagline: Three separate hard minutes, spread through your day.
modalities.whatItIs: Scattered Hard Minutes is a proposed way to fit hard effort into a busy day as three short, separate bursts instead of one session. Endurance training is one long, steady effort; this breaks the work into brief, precisely placed fragments, set up with a coach at first. Each burst has its own short warm-up.
modalities.coreIdea: Hard effort does not have to come in one block, and a few well-placed minutes can fit where a full workout cannot.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a coach you choose three slots in your day, such as before breakfast, at lunch and after work, and one simple mode, such as a stationary bike, brisk uphill walking or fast step-ups on a low step. At each slot you warm up for two to three minutes, go hard for one minute and then ease off for a minute or two. A weekly check-in with the coach adjusts the slots and the effort.
modalities.whoItsFor: Busy people who cannot find 30 minutes in one go, and anyone who finds a full session daunting.
modalities.cautions: Do not skip the short warm-up before each burst, since going hard from cold is harder on the heart and muscles, and get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain or high blood pressure. Stop at chest pain or dizziness and avoid bursts right after a large meal; it is a new idea with no research behind it.
modalities.tweet: Can't find 30 minutes? A novel idea: Scattered Hard Minutes. Three times a day, warm up for 2 to 3 minutes, go hard for one minute (bike, uphill walk, step-ups), then ease off. Hard effort in fragments instead of one block.

modalities.name: Weightless Water Sprints
modalities.tagline: Hard interval effort in water, with no load and no impact.
modalities.whatItIs: Weightless Water Sprints moves hard intervals into the water, with hard lengths of swimming or deep-water running and rests at the wall, so the water carries the body while the heart and lungs work hard. Strength training builds muscle by lifting heavy loads; this proposed session has no weights and almost no impact, aiming the effort entirely at the heart and lungs. It suits a public pool with a lifeguard.
modalities.coreIdea: Taking load and impact out of hard effort leaves pure heart-and-lungs work that is gentle on the joints yet still intense.
modalities.whatYouDo: After 10 minutes of easy swimming, swim one length hard, or run hard in the deep end with a flotation belt for 30 to 45 seconds, then rest at the wall for 45 to 90 seconds. Repeat eight to twelve times, then swim easily for five minutes. Less confident swimmers can do the whole session as deep-water running in a lane near the side.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose joints complain about running or jumping, and anyone who wants hard cardio without lifting or pounding.
modalities.cautions: Never train hard in water alone: use a lifeguarded pool, stay near the side and stop if you feel unusually breathless, faint or chilled. Get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting, high blood pressure or a seizure disorder; the concept itself is untested.
modalities.tweet: Hard intervals, zero impact: Weightless Water Sprints, an experimental idea. Swim one hard length (or run in the deep end with a float belt), rest at the wall, repeat eight to twelve times. Lifeguarded pool only. Easy on joints, hard on lungs. 🏊

modalities.name: Bare-Floor Circuit
modalities.tagline: Hard intervals anywhere, with nothing but your body and a timer.
modalities.whatItIs: Bare-Floor Circuit is an untested self-led interval circuit that needs no equipment, partner, coach or app, just your body, a little floor space and a kitchen timer. Animal-assisted therapy brings a living companion and a professional team into the room; this is complete self-sufficiency, with no one and nothing else involved. It is fully structured and can be done anywhere.
modalities.coreIdea: When the only equipment is your own body, there is nothing to arrange and no one to wait for, so hard exercise becomes possible anywhere.
modalities.whatYouDo: After five minutes of marching on the spot and gentle squats, cycle through four moves for 30 seconds each at hard effort, such as fast squats, step-ups on a bottom stair, mountain climbers and fast high-knee marching, with 30 seconds of rest after each. Rest two minutes after each round and do three or four rounds. Finish with a slow walk around the room and some stretching.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with no gym, little time or an irregular schedule, and anyone who likes not depending on anyone or anything to exercise.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and choose low-impact moves if your knees, hips or back complain. Clear the floor of trip hazards, keep your form tidy, stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain and rest between hard days; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Gear-free and companion-free: Bare-Floor Circuit, a new idea. Fast squats, stair step-ups, mountain climbers and high knees, 30 seconds hard each, 30 seconds rest, three or four rounds. A kitchen timer is the only equipment.

modalities.name: Standstill Bursts
modalities.tagline: From total stillness to maximum power in a few seconds.
modalities.whatItIs: Standstill Bursts is a proposed interval session of explosive efforts from a near stop: 6 to 10 seconds of all-out acceleration on a stationary bike, each followed by long, full recovery. Qigong moves slowly, softly and smoothly, and this is its explosive opposite. The bike keeps impact low while the effort stays as intense as it gets.
modalities.coreIdea: Going from stillness to full power as fast as possible is practice in explosive force, the far opposite of slow, flowing movement.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up on a stationary bike with moderate resistance, slow almost to a stop, then accelerate as hard as you can for 6 to 10 seconds. Pedal very easily for two to three minutes until fully recovered, then repeat six to eight times. Cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy short, intense challenges, and anyone who wants to build power and feel strong without heavy lifting.
modalities.cautions: Explosive efforts briefly push blood pressure and heart rate very high, so get medical advice first if you have heart disease, high blood pressure or a history of stroke, and keep breathing rather than holding your breath during bursts. Build up over weeks from moderate starts, set the bike up correctly and stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain; as a new concept, it has no track record yet.
modalities.tweet: From stillness to full power in a few seconds: Standstill Bursts, a speculative practice. On a bike, accelerate as hard as you can from a near stop for 6 to 10 seconds, then pedal easily for 2 to 3 minutes. Six to eight times.

modalities.name: Dawn Solo Ritual
modalities.tagline: A fixed, private interval session before the social day begins.
modalities.whatItIs: Dawn Solo Ritual is a solitary interval idea for early mornings, before anyone else needs you, following a coach-written script that never varies, with no talk, screens or company. Socializing is open, unscripted time with people; this is a private, silent and tightly scripted ritual of hard effort. It runs on two or three set mornings a week.
modalities.coreIdea: A fixed, solitary session at the start of the day carves out time that belongs only to you, before the day's contact and demands begin.
modalities.whatYouDo: On your set mornings, get up at the same time, drink some water and follow the same script: 10 minutes of gradual warm-up, eight 30-second hard bouts of jump rope or stationary cycling with 90 seconds easy between, and 10 minutes of cool-down. The phone stays on silent, face down, until the ritual is complete. A coach writes the script at the start and reviews it once a month.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose days are full of other people's needs, such as parents or carers, and anyone who wants a protected start to the morning.
modalities.cautions: Muscles and joints are stiffer early in the morning, so never skip the full warm-up, and get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure. Keep easy days between sessions, stop at chest pain or dizziness and keep your silenced phone within reach; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Before the house wakes up, a ritual that's only yours. Dawn Solo Ritual is a new concept: same time, same coach-written script, phone on silent, eight hard 30-second bouts with a full warm-up and cool-down. Two or three mornings a week. 🌅

modalities.name: Indoor Exact Hills
modalities.tagline: The hill, brought indoors and made exact by a coach.
modalities.whatItIs: Indoor Exact Hills is a proposed coach-programmed treadmill session in which every hard bout has an exact incline and speed, in a climate-controlled room, so that only your effort varies. Hiking and nature walks are open, unpredictable and full of the outdoors; this is indoors, controlled and measured to the decimal. The coach adjusts the numbers as you progress.
modalities.coreIdea: Removing every outside variable (weather, terrain, route) makes effort and progress precise and easy to compare from week to week.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up walk, the coach's plan sets each bout, such as 45 seconds at a steep incline and a brisk speed, followed by 90 seconds of flat, slow walking. You repeat six to ten bouts, holding the handrails only lightly for balance, then cool down for 10 minutes. Every two weeks the coach nudges the incline or the speed up a notch if you are ready.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who prefer predictable conditions, live where outdoor training is hard, or want a precisely measured program built for them.
modalities.cautions: Steep, fast treadmill work strains the heart, calves and Achilles tendons, so get medical advice first if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and build up gradually. Learn the emergency stop and use the safety clip, and stop at chest pain or dizziness; the idea itself has not been studied.
modalities.tweet: A hill with no weather, no mud and exact numbers. Indoor Exact Hills is a hypothetical program: a coach sets the incline and speed for every 45-second treadmill bout and nudges them up as you progress. For lovers of predictable conditions.

modalities.name: One-Word Bouts
modalities.tagline: Each hard bout steered by a single silent cue word.
modalities.whatItIs: One-Word Bouts is a small-group interval class idea in which a coach gives one short cue word for each hard bout, such as 'tall', 'drive' or 'quick', and you repeat it silently to steer your form and focus. Sensory mindfulness rests on plain sensing without steering anything; this leads attention deliberately with a chosen word. It is coached, fully structured and sociable.
modalities.coreIdea: A single well-chosen word can hold attention and technique together when effort is too intense for detailed instructions.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a group of four to eight, the coach leads a warm-up and then eight bouts of 40 seconds hard on bikes, rowers or a running track, with 80 seconds easy between. Before each bout the coach names the cue word and what it means, such as 'tall' for an upright posture, and you repeat it silently in rhythm with your effort. At the end, each person shares which word helped most.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds wander or whose form falls apart when they get tired, and anyone who enjoys a coached group with a clear focus.
modalities.cautions: Check with a doctor before starting if you have heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, and work at your own effort rather than matching the group. Stop at chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain and keep easy days between hard sessions; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: 'Tall.' 'Drive.' 'Quick.' One-Word Bouts is a prototype class: before each hard 40-second bout, the coach gives one cue word, and you repeat it silently to steer your form and focus. Small group, eight bouts, a word for each.

modalities.name: No-Soundtrack Intervals
modalities.tagline: Hard intervals with no music, only your own breath and steps.
modalities.whatItIs: No-Soundtrack Intervals is a proposed interval session done with no music, podcast or headphones, so the only soundtrack is your own breathing, footsteps and heartbeat. Music shapes effort with someone else's rhythm and mood; this lets both the rhythm and the effort come entirely from your own body. It is self-led and fully structured.
modalities.coreIdea: Without a playlist to carry you, you can hear your effort directly, and your breathing becomes the gauge of how hard you are working.
modalities.whatYouDo: Run, row or cycle with no audio at all: warm up for 10 minutes, then do six hard 2-minute bouts with 2 minutes easy between. Use the sound of your breath as the gauge, heavy and loud in the hard bouts, and listen to it settle during each recovery. In the last bout, notice the rhythm your steps or strokes fall into on their own.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who never exercise without headphones and want to try it unplugged, and anyone who wants to learn to read their own effort.
modalities.cautions: Anyone with heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure should get medical advice before hard intervals, and everyone should build up gradually with easy days between sessions. Being unplugged outdoors helps you hear traffic, but still choose safe routes, and stop at chest pain or dizziness; nothing about it has been tested yet.
modalities.tweet: Leave the headphones at home. No-Soundtrack Intervals is an untested idea: six hard 2-minute bouts with nothing in your ears but your own breath and footsteps, listening to your breathing settle in each recovery. Learn to hear your own effort.
